CHAPTER  2:  PEN  DESIGN  &  HOUSING  
Your  poultry  house  is  not  just  a  shelter;  it  is  the  environment  where  your  birds  will  live,  grow,  and  produce  profit.  A  poorly  
designed
 
pen
 
leads
 
to
 
heat
 
stress,
 
respiratory
 
disease,
 
poor
 
feed
 
conversion,
 
and
 
high
 
mortality.
 
A
 
well-designed
 
pen
 
pays
 
for
 
itself
 
many
 
times
 
over.
 
2.1   Site  Selection  —  Where  to  Build  
•
 
📍
 
Choose
 
elevated,
 
well-drained
 
land.
 
Avoid
 
low-lying
 
or
 
flood-prone
 
areas
 
—
 
wet
 
ground
 
=
 
disease.
 
•
 
📍
 
Minimum
 
500
 
metres
 
from
 
residential
 
areas
 
to
 
avoid
 
community
 
complaints
 
about
 
odour
 
and
 
disease
 
risk.
 
•
 
📍
 
Ensure
 
road
 
access
 
for
 
feed
 
delivery
 
and
 
bird
 
collection
 
trucks.
 
•
 
📍
 
Adequate
 
clean
 
water
 
supply
 
(borehole
 
or
 
pipe-borne).
 
•
 
📍
 
Away
 
from
 
other
 
livestock
 
farms,
 
wild
 
bird
 
habitats,
 
or
 
abattoirs
 
—
 
all
 
are
 
biosecurity
 
threats.
 
•
 
📍
 
Orient
 
the
 
house
 
on
 
an
 
East-West
 
axis
 
so
 
the
 
length
 
faces
 
north
 
and
 
south.
 
This
 
controls
 
direct
 
sunlight
 
from
 
entering
 
the
 
pen
 
while
 
maximizing
 
cross-ventilation
 
through
 
the
 
open
 
sides.
 
2.2   Types  of  Poultry  Housing  in  Nigeria  
House  Type Description Best  For Cost 
Open-Sided  (Deep  Litter)  Open  wire  mesh  or  wood  slatted  sides;  birds  on  a  bedded  floor.  Relies  on  natural  ventilation.  Small  to  medium  farms  (100–5,000  birds)  Low–Medium  
Semi-Closed  (Curtain-sided)  
Sides  have  adjustable  curtains/tarpaulin  for  climate  control.  Better  temperature  management.  Medium  farms  in  hot-season  regions  Medium  
Closed/Controlled  Environment  
Fully  enclosed  with  mechanical  ventilation,  cooling  pads,  and  exhaust  fans.  Full  temperature  control.  Large-scale  farms  (10,000+  birds)  High  
Battery  Cage  System  Birds  in  wire  cages  stacked  vertically.  Common  for  layers,  less  used  for  broilers  in  Nigeria.  Layer  production  mainly  High  
 
✅
 
Recommended
 
for
 
Beginners 
Start  with  the  Open-Sided  Deep  Litter  System.  It  is  low-cost,  easy  to  manage,  and  well-suited  to  Nigeria's  warm  climate.  A  width  no  more  than  8–9  metres  (25–30  ft)  to  allow  natural  cross-ventilation  to  reach  the  centre  of  the  house.  
2.3   Key  Design  Specifications  
Component Specification Why  It  Matters 
Orientation  East-West  (length  axis)  Prevents  direct  sunlight  from  beating  into  open  sides;  maximizes  north-south  cross-ventilation  
Width  7–9  metres  (max  9  m  /  30  ft)  for  open-sided  Wider  houses  have  poor  ventilation  at  the  centre,  causing  heat  buildup  and  ammonia  accumulation  
Length  Any,  based  on  the  bird  count  Calculate:  1  sq.  ft  per  bird  (0.093  m²).  For  500  birds  =  ~500  sq.  ft  /  ~46  m²

2.5   Bedding  (Litter)  Materials  
Litter  Material Advantages Disadvantages 
Rice  Husk  Widely  available,  absorbent,  cheap,  and  good  insulation  Can  harbour  mould  if  wet;  chicks  eat  it  if  not  covered  with  brooder  paper  initially  
Wood  Shavings  Excellent  absorbency,  fluffy  and  comfortable,  widely  used  Must  be  sourced  clean;  avoid  treated  wood  with  chemicals  
Sawdust  Very  fine  —  absorbs  quickly  
Can  be  too  dusty,  high  CRD  risk;  higher  coccidiosis  and  risk  if  wet;  avoid  as  sole  litter  
Chopped  Straw  Available  in  some  regions  Poor  moisture  absorption;  can  pack  into  a  hard  mat  
Newspapers  (brooder  layer)  Good  starter  cover  for  the  first  3–5  days  over  litter  Not  a  litter  material;  used  only  as  a  top  layer  for  day-old  chicks  
 
⚠
 
WARNING
 
—
 
Do
 
NOT
 
Use
 
Tarpaulin 
Never  use  tarpaulin  as  a  floor  cover  instead  of  brooder  paper.  Tarpaulin  is  waterproof  and  holds  moisture  against  the  bedding,  creating  the  perfect  environment  for  coccidia  to  multiply.  This  directly  causes  early-age  coccidiosis  and  elevated  mortality.

Chick  feeders  (tray/shallow)  4–6  Use  only  shallow  trays  in  Week  1.  Chicks  can't  reach  deep  feeders  
Tube  feeders  (3  kg)  or  Iron  feeders  4–6  Week  2  onwards,  keep  the  edge  at  the  bird's  back  height

CHAPTER  3:  BROILER  BREEDS  —  WHICH  TO  CHOOSE?  
One  of  the  most  confusing  areas  for  new  farmers  in  Nigeria  is  the  difference  between  a  breed  name  and  a  hatchery  name.  
Understanding
 
this
 
distinction
 
will
 
help
 
you
 
make
 
a
 
smarter
 
decision
 
when
 
sourcing
 
your
 
chicks.
 
HATCHERY  vs.  BREED  —  Know  the  Difference 
A  hatchery  (e.g.,  Agrited,  CHI,  Zartech)  is  the  company  that  hatches  and  sells  day-old  chicks.  
A  breed  (e.g.,  Ross  308,  Cobb  500,  Arbor  Acres)  is  the  genetic  line  of  the  bird.   
One  hatchery  can  switch  breeds  over  time.  Always  ask:  ‘What  breed  are  these  chicks?’ ,  not  just  ‘Where  are  they  from?’  
3.1   The  Main  Broiler  Breeds  in  Nigeria  
The  five  most  common  commercial  broiler  breeds  used  in  Nigeria  are  described  below.  
①
 
COBB
 
500
 
—
 
The
 
Farmer's
 
Favourite
 
The  Cobb  500,  produced  by  Cobb-Vantress  (USA,  founded  1916),  is  the  world's  most  widely  used  commercial  broiler  breed  and  
is
 
the
 
top
 
choice
 
for
 
many
 
Nigerian
 
farmers,
 
particularly
 
those
 
in
 
warm,
 
tropical
 
regions.
 
Bred
 
by
 
Zartech,
 
Chikun
 
(Olam),
 
Cascada,
 
etc.
 
Feature Detail 
Growth  rate  Excellent  —  among  the  fastest  in  tropical  conditions  
Feed  conversion  ratio  (FCR)  Very  good  —  performs  well  even  on  lower-cost,  lower-density  feed  
Market  weight  (6  weeks)  ~2.0–2.4  kg  under  good  management  
Market  weight  (8  weeks)  ~2.5–3.0  kg  under  good  management  
Heat  tolerance  Good  —  handles  Nigerian  hot  climate  well  
Leg  strength  Strong  bones;  good  livability  
Carcass  yield  Excellent  breast  meat;  high  dressing  percentage  
Disease  sensitivity  Slightly  sensitive  —  requires  good  management.  Susceptible  to  CRD  
Sudden  death  syndrome  Slightly  higher  risk  due  to  fast  growth  —  monitor  closely  
Best  for  All  market  types:  live  weight,  processors,  small  to  large  farms  
 
Research  Verdict 
Multiple  Nigerian  university  studies  comparing  Cobb  500,  Ross  308,  and  Arbor  Acres  in  tropical  conditions  consistently  found  Cobb  500  to  outperform  on  body  weight,  weight  gain,  feed  conversion  ratio,  carcass  weight,  and  breast  meat  yield.  It  is  the  top  recommendation  for  Nigerian  broiler  farmers.  
 
②
 
ROSS
 
308
 
—
 
The
 
Global
 
Performer
 
The  Ross  308,  produced  by  Aviagen  (UK/USA),  is  arguably  the  world's  most  widely  distributed  broiler  breed.  It  is  used  heavily  in  
large
 
commercial
 
operations
 
globally
 
and
 
is
 
available
 
through
 
Agrited
 
and
 
Sayed
 
hatcheries
 
in
 
Nigeria.

CHAPTER  4:  DETAILED  BROODING  GUIDE  (Days  0–14)  
Brooding  is  the  most  critical  phase  of  your  entire  production  cycle.  Studies  consistently  show  that  60–80%  of  total  broiler  
mortality
 
happens
 
in
 
the
 
first
 
two
 
weeks.
 
Master
 
brooding,
 
and
 
you
 
have
 
secured
 
most
 
of
 
your
 
profit.
 
4.1   What  is  Brooding?  
Brooding  is  the  artificial  provision  of  heat,  light,  water,  and  feed  to  mimic  the  warmth  and  protection  a  mother  hen  would  give  
her
 
chicks.
 
Day-old
 
chicks
 
cannot
 
regulate
 
their
 
own
 
body
 
temperature
 
(they
 
are
 
homeotherms
 
but
 
not
 
yet
 
thermoregulating).
 
They
 
rely
 
entirely
 
on
 
external
 
heat.
 
Without
 
adequate
 
brooding,
 
chicks
 
pile
 
up,
 
become
 
chilled,
 
and
 
die
 
often
 
within
 
the
 
first
 
48–72
 
hours.
 
4.2   Pre-Arrival  Preparation  (7  Days  Before  Chicks  Arrive)  
Preparation  is  not  optional.  The  7-day  timeline  below  is  the  minimum.  Well-prepared  farms  have  far  lower  Day-1  mortality.  
Days   Before  Arrival Task Detail 
Day  7  Clean  the  pen  thoroughly  
Remove  all  old  litter,  feathers,  dust,  and  droppings  from  the  previous  batch.  Scrape  floors  and  walls.  Remember,  the  pen  is  meant  to  rest  for  at  least  2  weeks  before  the  new  batch.  
Day  7  Disinfect  pen  
Use  a  broad-spectrum  disinfectant  (Vinkokill,  Iodophor,  Povidone  Iodine,  or  a  combination  of  formalin  and  permanganate  in  the  ratio  of  3:2).  Spray  all  surfaces:  floor,  walls,  roof,  feeders,  and  drinkers.  Leave  empty  to  air-dry  for  a  minimum  of  48  hours.  
Day  5–6  Rest  period  Keep  the  pen  closed  and  empty.  Allows  residual  pathogens  to  die  off.  No  entry  without  a  footbath.  
Day  3–4  Set  up  litter  
Spread  7–10  cm  (3–4  inches)  of  clean,  dry  litter  (rice  husk  or  wood  shavings)  evenly  over  the  floor.  Use  the  disinfectant  to  spray  lightly  on  the  litter  and  allow  it  to  air  dry.  
Day  2–3  Place  brooder  paper  Lay  clean  newspaper  or  brooder  paper  over  the  litter  to  cover  the  entire  brooding  area.  Tape  edges  so  chicks  cannot  crawl  under  it.  
Day  1  Install  feeders  and  drinkers  Position  feeders  and  drinkers  inside  the  brooder  circle.  Ratio:  1  drinker  and  1  shallow  feeder  per  25  chicks  minimum.  
Day  1   (24hrs  before  arrival)  Set  up  and  test  the  heat  source  Turn  on  the  heat  source.  Measure  temperature  at  the  chick  level  with  a  thermometer.  Adjust  until  32–35°C  is  stable.  Do  NOT  wait  until  chicks  arrive  to  test  your  heat  source.  
Day  1  Prepare  an  antistress  solution  
Mix  glucose  (50g)  +  Vitamin  C  per  5  litres  of  lukewarm  water,  OR  prepare  a  commercial  antistress  solution.  Have  them  ready  to  give  chicks  within  minutes  of  arrival.

4.3   Temperature  Management  
Temperature  is  the  single  most  controllable  factor  in  brooding.  Too  cold  and  chicks  pile  up  and  suffocate  or  develop  respiratory  
infections.
 
Too
 
hot
 
and
 
they
 
pant,
 
dehydrate,
 
and
 
stop
 
eating.
 
Age  (Days) Required  Temperature  at  Chick  Level Signs  It's  Correct 
Day  1–3  33–35°C  Chicks  move  freely  under  and  around  the  heat  source;  normal  chirping  (chick  sound)  
Day  4–7  32–33°C  Even  distribution  in  the  pen,  active  feeding  and  drinking  
Week  2  (Days  8–14)  29–32°C  (reduce  ~2.5°C  per  week)  Chicks  spread  throughout  the  brooder;  comfortable  
Week  3  (Days  15–21)  27–29°C  Still  warm,  but  no  cold  stress  signs  
Week  4+  24–27°C  Feathers  are  fully  developed;  less  artificial  heat  is  needed  
Week  5–6  24–26°C  or  ambient  if  >24°C  Birds  are  fully  feathered;  heat  stress  management  begins  
4.4   Reading  Chick  Behaviour  —  Your  Best  Thermometer  
Even  with  a  thermometer,  observe  your  chicks  constantly.  Behaviour  tells  you  what  the  temperature  feels  like  to  them  —  not  
just
 
what
 
it
 
reads.
 
Behaviour What  It  Means Corrective  Action 
Chicks  huddle  tightly  under  the  heat  source  TOO  COLD  Lower  the  heat  source  to  the  chick  level  if  you  are  using  electric  bulbs  or  increase  intensity;  check  for  drafts  
Chicks  are  spread  evenly  throughout  the  brooder  PERFECT  TEMPERATURE  ✅  No  action  needed  —  this  is  your  target  
Chicks  move  away  from  the  heat  source,  panting  TOO  HOT  Raise  the  heat  source;  open  the  curtains;  reduce  the  temperature  
Chicks  crowd  to  one  side  of  the  brooder  DRAFT/WIND  from  one  side  Block  the  wind  source;  check  curtains  and  openings  
Loud,  continuous  distress  chirping  Discomfort  (cold,  hungry,  thirsty,  or  sick)  Check  all  conditions:  temperature,  water,  feed  
Soft,  contentment  peeping  Comfortable  ✅  Good  sign  —  keep  conditions  stable  
Pasty  vent  (dirty  droppings  stuck  to  rear)  Chilled  or  dehydrated  Gently  clean  the  vent  with  warm  water;  warm  up  the  pen;  rehydrate  
Lethargy,  eyes  closed,  not  moving  Severe  cold  stress  or  illness  Emergency:  warm  up  pen;  call  your  vet  
 
4.5   Feeding  and  Water  in  the  First  14  Days

Water  First  —  Always 
When  chicks  arrive,  they  are  dehydrated  from  the  stress  of  transportation.  The  number  one  rule  is:  water  before  feed.  Give  antistress  or  glucose  water  for  a  minimum  of  1–2  hours  before  introducing  feed.  Cold  water  causes  intestinal  shock.  Always  use  lukewarm  water  for  day-old  chicks.

4.6   Lighting  Programme  for  Broilers  
Age Light  Hours Purpose 
Days  1–7  23  hours  light  /  1  hour  dark  Encourage  maximum  feeding  and  drinking;  support  growth  and  adaptation  
Days  8–14  20  hours  light  /  4  hours  dark  Begin  a  mild  dark  period;  reduces  leg  stress  from  continuous  activity  
Week  3  onwards  18–20  hours  light  /  4–6  hours  dark  Balanced  light  for  growth;  allows  proper  bone  development  
Week  5–8  16–18  hours  light  /  6–8  hours  dark  Maintain  appetite  and  growth  in  the  finishing  phase  
 
ALTERNATIVELY 
If  your  target  is  to  sell  the  birds  between  5-6  weeks,  give  23  hours  of  light  and  1  hour  of  darkness  for  longer  feeding  hours  and  maximum  growth.

CHAPTER  7:  BIOSECURITY  &  DISEASE  PREVENTION  
Biosecurity  is  your  invisible  fence  between  your  flock  and  the  diseases  that  can  wipe  it  out.  It  costs  almost  nothing,  but  poor

Entry  Rule How  to  Apply 
Footbath  at  every  entrance  Keep  a  footbath  with  an  active  disinfectant  (change  solution  every  day).  Everyone  who  enters  must  step  through  it.  
Limit  visitors  No  visitors  unless  necessary.  Visitors  =  disease  vectors.  
Change  clothing  before  entering  Keep  farm-specific  clothes  and  boots  at  the  gate.  Change  before  entering  the  pen.  
No  cross-farm  movement  Never  visit  another  poultry  farm  and  then  enter  your  pen  without  changing  clothes  and  showering.  
Vehicle  biosecurity  Spray  the  tyres  of  incoming  vehicles,  especially  feed  delivery  trucks,  with  disinfectant.  
Wild  bird  exclusion  Cover  open  sides  with  wire  mesh  fine  enough  to  keep  sparrows  and  other  wild  birds  out.  Wild  birds  carry  Newcastle  disease  and  avian  influenza.  
Rodent  control  Set  bait  stations  at  the  perimeter.  Rats  carry  Salmonella  and  destroy  feed.  Seal  all  gaps  in  the  pen  structure.  
7.3   Sanitation  Routine  
Frequency Sanitation  Task 
Daily  Wash  and  scrub  all  drinkers.  Clean  feeders  of  wet  or  caked  feed.  Remove  dead  birds  immediately.  
Daily  Replace  wet  or  soiled  litter  spots.  Wet  litter  =  ammonia  =  respiratory  disease.  
Weekly  Spray  pen  with  dilute  disinfectant  (outside  business  hours/low  bird  disturbance).  
Every  batch  Full  cleanout:  remove  all  litter,  wash  and  disinfect  floors,  walls,  and  equipment.  Rest  pen  for  at  least  14  days  before  the  next  batch.  
Carcass  disposal  Never  throw  dead  birds  in  the  open.  Burn  or  bury  them  away  from  the  pen,  at  least  100  metres  away.

CHAPTER  9:  COMMON  POULTRY  DISEASES  —  QUICK  REFERENCE  
9.1   Viral  Diseases  
⚠
 
CRITICAL:
 
Viral
 
Diseases
 
Have
 
NO
 
Cure 
Viral  diseases  (Newcastle,  IBD/Gumboro,  Fowl  Pox,  Marek's,  Infectious  Bronchitis)  cannot  be  treated  with  any  drug.  The  virus  must  run  its  course.  Your  only  defences  are:  vaccination  BEFORE  infection,  immune  support  during  outbreak,  and  strict  biosecurity  to  prevent  spread.  Never  let  anyone  sell  you  a  ‘cure’  for  viral  disease;  it  does  not  exist.  
 
Disease Cause Key  Signs  Farmers  Will  Notice Prevention  /  First  Response 
Newcastle  Disease  (ND)  Newcastle  Disease  Virus  (NDV)  
Young  birds:  gasping,  twisted  neck,  green  diarrhea.  Adults:  egg  drop,  paralysis,  coughing.  Spreads  via  air,  equipment,  and  farm  visitors.  No  cure.  Isolate  sick  birds  immediately.  Contact  vet.  Bury  dead  birds.  PREVENT  with  the  Lasota  vaccine  on  schedule.  
Gumboro  /  IBD  Infectious  Bursal  Disease  Virus  
Watery  white  diarrhea,  birds  sit  and  refuse  to  move,  vent  pecking,  and  dehydration.  Rapid  deaths  from  Day  14–21  if  unvaccinated.  
No  cure.  Start  multivitamins  +  electrolytes.  Control  secondary  infections  with  antibiotics  under  vet  supervision.  Disinfect  aggressively.  PREVENT  with  the  Gumboro  vaccine.  
Marek's  Disease  Alphaherpesvirus  
Sudden  leg  paralysis;  one  leg  stretched  forward,  one  backward;  progressive  weakness.  Buy  only  vaccinated  chicks.  Vaccinate  at  the  hatchery  or  Day  1.  Isolate  affected  birds.  Cannot  be  treated.  
Fowl  Pox  
Fowl  Pox  Virus  (spread  by  mosquitoes)  Dry  form:  black  scabs  on  the  comb  and  wattles.  Wet  form:  white  plaques  in  the  mouth,  birds  gasp.  Vaccinate  on  time.  Control  mosquitoes  and  flies.  Isolate  infected  birds.  Disinfect  surfaces.  
Infectious  Bronchitis  (IB)  Coronavirus  (avian)  Gasping,  coughing,  watery  eyes,  and  reduced  egg  production  in  layers.  Can  predispose  to  E.  coli  infection.  No  direct  cure.  Manage  with  supportive  care  and  antibiotics  for  secondary  infections  under  veterinary  supervision.

Disease Cause Key  Signs First  Response  /  Control

Isolate  sick  birds.  Improve  ventilation.  Antibiotics  (Tylosin/Enrofloxacin)  help  control,  but  the  carrier  state  remains.  Consult  your  vet.

CHAPTER  10:  BROILER  FLOCK  UNIFORMITY  
Most  broiler  farmers  weigh  their  birds  at  market  only  to  discover  some  are  1.2  kg,  and  others  are  2.4  kg.  That  gap  is  lost  money.

10.2   How  to  Calculate  Broiler  Flock  Uniformity  —  Step  by  Step  
You  need:  a  digital  hanging  or  platform  scale,  a  notebook,  and  at  least  10%  of  your  flock  sampled  randomly.  
Step What  to  Do Example 
Step  1  Pick  birds  at  random  —  do  not  hand-pick  the  biggest  or  smallest.  Catch  from  different  parts  of  the  pen.  Flock  of  200  birds  →  weigh  20  birds  at  random  
Step  2  Weigh  each  bird  individually.  Write  every  weight  down.  
Weights  (g):  1800,  1750,  1900,  1650,  1820,  1780,  1760,  1830,  1700,  1860,  1790,  1840,  1720,  1810,  1880,  1740,  1770,  1850,  1690,  1810  
Step  3  Add  all  weights  together.  Divide  by  the  number  of  birds  weighed  to  get  the  average.  Total  =  35,900  g  ÷  20  birds  =  1,795  g  average  
Step  4  Calculate  ±10%  of  the  average.  This  is  your  acceptable  range.  10%  of  1,795  =  179  g.   Lower  limit:  1,795  −  179  =  1,616  g.   Upper  limit:  1,795  +  179  =  1,974  g  
Step  5  Count  how  many  birds  fall  between  the  lower  and  upper  limit.  18  out  of  20  birds  are  within  1,616–1,974  g  
Step  6  Calculate:  (Birds  within  range  ÷  Total  birds  weighed)  ×  100  (18  ÷  20)  ×  100  =  90%  uniformity

Uniformity  % Rating What  It  Means Action

75%  –  84%  Good  🟡  Minor  variation.  Acceptable  for  most  farms.  Check  feeder  access  and  water  distribution.  Monitor  closely.  
65%  –  74%  Poor  🟠  Significant  variation.  Investigate  immediately.  Check  for  disease,  crowding,  feeder  competition,  and  feed  quality.

What  Is  a  Good  Profit  Margin  for  Broilers? 
A  well-managed  broiler  batch  in  Nigeria  should  yield  a  profit  margin  of  25–40%  and  an  ROI  of  40–70%  per  cycle.  If  your  margin  is  below  20%,  investigate  your  feed  cost  first  (it  is  your  biggest  variable),  then  your  mortality  rate,  then  your  selling  price.  Most  losses  trace  back  to  one  of  these  three  factors.

If  you  are  running  a  batch  in  this  rainy-season  cycle,  remember  from  Chapter  13  that  there  is  no  festive  period  (Christmas,  Easter,  Eid)  to  fall  back  on  for  a  price  boost.  That  makes  it  even  more  important  to  protect  your  flock  through  the  rains,   a  healthy,  uniform  batch  sold  efficiently  is  the  only  thing  standing  between  you  and  a  thin  margin  this  cycle.  
14.1   Why  the  Rainy  Season  Is  High-Risk  for  Broilers  
Rainy-Season  Factor What  It  Does  to  Your  Birds 
High  humidity  Litter  absorbs  moisture  and  stays  wet  far  longer  than  in  dry  season.  Wet  litter  is  the  No.1  trigger  for  coccidiosis  and  ammonia  build-up.  
Day–night  temperature  swings  Hot,  humid  afternoons  followed  by  cool,  wet  nights  stress  birds'  thermoregulation,  weakening  immunity  and  triggering  respiratory  disease.  
Reduced  sunlight/drying  time  Litter,  feed  bags,  and  equipment  that  get  damp  take  much  longer  to  dry  out,  extending  the  window  for  mould  and  bacteria  to  grow.  
More  frequent  power  outages  Storms  increase  grid  failures.  A  heat-lamp  or  gas  brooder  losing  power  on  a  wet,  cool  night  is  far  more  dangerous  than  the  same  outage  in  dry  season.  
Increased  mosquito  breeding  Standing  water  around  the  pen  multiplies  mosquito  populations,  raising  the  risk  of  Fowl  Pox  (Chapter  9.1).  
Feed  and  litter  spoilage  risk  Damp  storage  conditions  promote  mould  growth  and  aflatoxin  (mycotoxin)  contamination  in  feed  and  litter  materials.  
Flooding  and  waterlogging  Low-lying  pens  or  poorly  drained  surroundings  can  let  rainwater  enter  the  house,  soaking  litter  and  stressing  birds  directly.  
Slippery,  delayed  logistics  Rain-affected  roads  delay  feed  deliveries  and  can  delay  buyers  picking  up  birds  on  harvest  day.

Position  the  heat  source  away  from  any  wall  or  roof  section  prone  to  leaking  A  heat  lamp  or  gas  brooder  getting  wet  is  both  a  chilling  risk  and  an  electrical/fire  hazard

APPENDIX:  GLOSSARY  OF  TERMS  
Quick  definitions  of  terms  used  throughout  this  toolkit.  
Term Definition 
Ad  libitum  Feed  or  water  made  available  at  all  times,  with  no  restriction  on  quantity.  
All-in,  all-out  A  biosecurity  system  where  an  entire  flock  is  placed  and  removed  together  —  no  mixing  of  ages  or  batches  in  the  same  pen.  
Anticoccidial  A  drug  used  to  prevent  or  treat  coccidiosis  (e.g.  Amprolium,  Toltrazuril,  Diclazuril).  
Antistress  solution  A  water-soluble  blend  of  vitamins,  electrolytes,  and/or  glucose  given  to  reduce  stress,  commonly  used  on  arrival  and  after  vaccination.  
Biosecurity  The  set  of  practices  used  to  prevent  disease-causing  organisms  from  entering  or  spreading  within  a  farm.  
Bird  density  /  Stocking  density  The  number  of  birds  per  unit  of  floor  area,  usually  expressed  per  square  metre  or  square  foot.  
Breed  The  genetic  line  of  a  bird  (e.g.  Cobb  500,  Ross  308,  Arbor  Acres)  —  distinct  from  the  hatchery  that  supplies  it.  
Broiler  A  chicken  raised  specifically  for  meat  production,  as  opposed  to  egg  production  (layer).  
Brooder  /  Brooding  The  heated  enclosure  and  the  process  of  providing  artificial  warmth  to  day-old  chicks  who  cannot  yet  regulate  their  own  body  temperature.  
Brooder  guard  A  circular  barrier  (cardboard,  wire,  or  plastic)  used  to  confine  chicks  near  the  heat  source  during  the  first  days  of  brooding.  
Carcass  yield  /  Dressing  percentage  The  proportion  of  a  bird's  live  weight  that  remains  as  usable  meat  after  slaughter  and  processing.  
Coccidiosis  A  common  intestinal  disease  caused  by  Eimeria  protozoa,  typically  linked  to  wet  litter.  
Cold  chain  The  unbroken  chain  of  refrigeration  required  to  keep  vaccines  effective  from  manufacture  to  administration.  
Crude  protein  (CP)  The  protein  content  of  a  feed,  expressed  as  a  percentage  —  a  key  indicator  of  feed  quality  at  each  growth  stage.  
Day-old  chick  (DOC)  A  newly  hatched  chick,  typically  24–48  hours  old,  as  supplied  by  a  hatchery.  
Dewormer  A  drug  given  to  eliminate  internal  parasites  (worms)  from  poultry.  
Eaves  height  The  height  of  the  side  walls  of  a  poultry  house,  measured  up  to  where  the  roof  begins.  
Eimeria  The  genus  of  protozoan  parasites  responsible  for  coccidiosis.  
Electrolytes  Mineral  salts  (sodium,  potassium,  bicarbonate,  etc.)  added  to  water  to  help  birds  maintain  fluid  balance,  especially  during  heat  or  disease  stress.

Footbath  A  shallow  container  of  disinfectant  solution  placed  at  entrances,  through  which  people  step  to  disinfect  their  footwear  before  entering  a  poultry  house.  
Free-range  A  system  in  which  birds  have  outdoor  access,  as  opposed  to  being  fully  housed.  
Hatchery  A  commercial  company  that  incubates  fertile  eggs  and  supplies  day-old  chicks  to  farmers.  
Litter  /  Bedding  Material  spread  on  the  floor  of  a  poultry  house  (e.g.  wood  shavings,  rice  husk)  to  absorb  moisture  and  droppings.  
Live  weight  The  weight  of  a  bird  while  still  alive,  before  slaughter  or  processing.  
Marek's  disease  A  viral  disease  causing  paralysis  in  young  birds,  prevented  through  hatchery-level  vaccination.  
Mortality  rate  The  percentage  of  birds  in  a  batch  that  die  during  the  production  cycle.  
Mycotoxin  A  toxic  compound  produced  by  mould  (fungus),  commonly  found  in  damp  or  poorly  stored  feed;  aflatoxin  is  a  well-known  example.  
Newcastle  Disease  (ND)  A  highly  contagious  viral  disease  affecting  the  respiratory,  nervous,  and  digestive  systems  of  poultry.  
Pasting  /  Pasty  vent  A  condition  where  droppings  stick  to  and  block  a  chick's  vent,  often  linked  to  chilling  or  dehydration.  
Probiotic  A  live  beneficial  microorganism  supplement  given  to  support  gut  health  and  digestion.  
Ridge  ventilation  An  opening  at  the  peak  of  a  roof  that  allows  rising  hot  air  and  ammonia  to  escape  from  a  poultry  house.  
Starter  feed  The  high-protein  feed  formulation  given  to  chicks  in  the  first  weeks  of  life.  
Stocking  density  See  Bird  density.  
Super  starter  feed  A  premium,  very  high-protein  feed  sometimes  used  in  the  first  1–2  weeks  before  transitioning  to  standard  starter  feed.  
Vaccination  route  The  method  by  which  a  vaccine  is  administered  —  commonly  eye-drop,  drinking  water,  or  injection.  
Vent  The  external  opening  through  which  a  bird  excretes  waste  and,  in  hens,  lays  eggs.  
Withdrawal  period  The  mandatory  time  after  the  last  drug  administration  during  which  a  bird  must  not  be  slaughtered  for  consumption,  to  allow  drug  residues  to  clear.
